# Tobit Chapter 14 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 14 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_014_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Tobit's words of praise came to an end. He was fifty-eight years old when he went blind. Eight years later his sight was restored. He spent the rest of his life giving generously to those in need, fearing the Lord his God, and never stopping his thanks.

**2** When he was very old and felt his end drawing near, he gathered his son Tobias and his six grandchildren and said to them, "Come close, all of you.

**3** I am old. I am ready to leave this life. Go to Media, my son — I believe with all my heart the words of the prophet Nahum about Nineveh. Everything he said will come true. Assyria will fall. Nineveh will fall. All of it — everything the prophets of Israel spoke, the ones God sent — it will all happen.

**4** Not a single word will go unfulfilled. Everything in its time. Media will be safer than Assyria or Babylon — trust me on this. I know it. I believe it. God's words do not come back empty.

**5** All our people in the land of Israel will be scattered, torn away from that good land. Israel will be desolate. Samaria will be desolate. Jerusalem will be desolate. The temple of God will be left in mourning and burned to the ground — for a time.

**6** "But then God will have mercy again. He will bring them back. He will bring our people home to the land of Israel, and they will rebuild the temple — not as glorious as before, not yet — not until the appointed time has been fully completed. After that, they will all come home from their exile. Jerusalem will be rebuilt, splendid and honored. The house of God will rise again in her, exactly as the prophets of Israel foretold.

**7** And then — all the nations, every people under heaven — they will turn. They will actually fear God. Truly, not merely with words. They will throw down their idols that have been lying to them for generations, and they will bless the God of all ages, righteously.

**8** All the sons of Israel who survive in those days — those who remember God and hold to him — will be gathered home. They will come to Jerusalem. They will live safely in the land of Abraham forever, and that land will be given to them. Those who truly love God will rejoice. Those who choose sin and injustice will be gone from the earth entirely.

**9** "So here is my charge to you, my children: serve God faithfully. Do what pleases him. And when you raise your own children, tell them the same: do right, give to those in need, remember God, bless his name at every moment — honestly, with everything you have.

**10** Leave Nineveh, my son. Nahum's words are certain — Nineveh's end is coming. Go to Media; you'll be safe there. Throughout my life I trusted Ahikar, and he stood by me into my old age. Do you remember what he did to his nephew Nadan, the one who tried to destroy him? Nadan dragged Ahikar down into darkness — but Ahikar came back up into the light. It was his generosity that saved him. Nadan set a deadly trap for Ahikar, but Ahikar's almsgiving pulled him free — and it was Nadan himself who stumbled into that trap and died.

**11** My children — remember that. See what generosity does. See what wickedness does: it kills its owner. Now — my soul is ready to go."

**12** They laid him down on his bed. He died. They buried him with full honor.

**13** When his mother Anna died, Tobias buried her beside his father. Then Tobias left with his wife and children for Ecbatana, to the home of his father-in-law Raguel.

**14** He grew old with grace and dignity, and when Raguel and Edna died, he buried them with honor too. He inherited everything — their estate and his father Tobit's estate as well.

**15** Tobias died in Ecbatana of Media at the age of ninety-nine. He lived long enough to hear the news — Nineveh had fallen. Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus had captured it. Before he drew his last breath, Tobias rejoiced.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

This is a deathbed scene, and it has to feel like one. An old man, gathered family, last words that are also prophecy. The weight of all that has happened — the blindness, the demon, the angel, the wedding, the healing — all of it distills into these final charges: serve God, give to those in need, leave this doomed city.

The prophecy embedded in vv. 3–8 is remarkable. Tobit predicts the Assyrian exile (already happened in the narrative), the destruction of Jerusalem (future in the story), the return from exile, the rebuilt temple, and then a final eschatological vision of all nations worshiping God. He is, in other words, a prophet — which the reader was perhaps not expecting from this domestic story about fish gall and a demon.

The Ahikar allusion (v. 10) is the book's final wisdom-tale within a tale: a nephew tried to destroy his benefactor-uncle, and it destroyed him instead. The moral is the moral of the whole book in miniature.

The last line is perfect. Tobias dies at 99, and his final act is to rejoice over Nineveh's destruction. The city that once held his family captive is gone. He saw it happen. That's the end of the story — justice, witnessed, in a lifetime. Not in the abstract. Tobias actually saw it.

— PNEUMA
